tone_statements.citation: Zidahwa Kavura, Emery [Nathan]. 2021. Kihavu Lexicon Compilation: Spelling and Basic Grammar. Research paper (memoire) for the degree of Licencie in English Language Teaching, Departement d'Anglais-Culture Africaine, Institut Superieur Pedagogique de Bukavu, academic year 2020-2021. xvii+136 pp. (154-page PDF); ch. 4 incl. section 4.3 'The tone', pp. 79-80.
tone_statements.quote: Kihavu is a two-tone high and low language. The high tone is marked by an acute accent that we have marked with the capital H, that is to say the voice is raised for this pronunciation, and for the low tone the voice is softened by downing the voice, that we have marked with the capital L. The falling intonation phenomenon is also attested within a lexeme number. The latter is marked by a small exclamation mark! [...] Let us point out that there are minimal pairs between two verbs or two nouns and which serve as examples of the lexical function of the tone: H.H.L kúshúka to lie H.L.L kúshuka to clean
tone_statements.locator: pp. 79-80, ch. 4, section 4.3 'The tone' and 4.3.3 'Tone function'
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: 2 level tones H vs L (L unmarked) with lexical and grammatical (tense/aspect) function, plus a lexeme-internal 'falling'/downstep marked '!'; noun tonal classes listed by surface melody; no mention of stress.

sources.note: Nothing. The phonology chapter describes three level tonemes (H, L, downstepped H) plus two contour tones and contrastive vowel quantity (2.18-19, 2.45, pp.23-25, 49), then intonation (2.46-50, pp.50-55): tonality = pitch at syllable level, intonation = pitch at phrase level; assertive intoneme = drop of pitch and intensity phrase-finally with devoicing of the last syllable.
